newsitem.title: USA: U.S. studies secondary market for community loans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. studies secondary market for community loans.

text.p: The Clinton administration is studying ways to package community development loans for sale to private investors and hopes to launch its first deal in the next six months, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Tuesday.

"My hope at least is in the next six months we will have accomplished the first of these poolings for resale and over the next few years we will develop a real secondary market," he told an urban policy forum here.
Rubin said such a step would help recycle capital back into the inner cities and depressed rural areas. "The power and leveraging are really very substantial," he said.
Speaking to reporters afterwards, Rubin said the initial deals would probably involve private placements with big investors such as insurance companies and pension funds.
"I don't think in the foreseeable future you'll see a trading secondary market," he said.
"But if you create a real private placement activity, that is an incredibly powerful instrument," he added.
Loans eligible for packaging would include credits extended by private borrowers, quasi-government agencies and government entities.
Not all inner-city loans would be eligible, and Rubin said the administration was concentrating on commercial credits rather than home mortgages.
He said many of the loan packages would require "credit enhancement" to entice investors.

Treasury officials said this could take the form of government guarantees or actual public funds that would effectively limit potential losses to investors in the loan pools. Charitable organizations might also contribute money to limit investor losses.
Commercial banks and local government agencies have already launched a handful of such deals, independent of Treasury and the Commerce Department.
Treasury officials said they were studying ways to encourage more standardization of terms on inner-city loans to help promote a secondary market.
